actions.body:
Recent progress in autonomous discovery systems highlights a critical divergence between task-specific automation and generalized scientific inquiry. The evidence suggests that while current models can simulate hypothesis generation and experimentation, they often lack the robustness required for the non-linear, failure-prone nature of authentic research. Systems like those described in the GOAL-Robots project emphasize the importance of self-generated goals as a lever for open-ended learning, allowing agents to navigate unpredictable environments. However, our synthesis reveals that for these systems to be truly autonomous, they must move beyond simple iteration to include meta-strategies for resource-constrained exploration. The transition to generalized discovery is currently bottlenecked by cascading dependencies in multi-file implementations and the difficulty of formalizing significance in self-generated problem spaces.

Summary
Autonomous inquiry systems face challenges in iterative experiment refinement and independent goal generation. To succeed, they require robust self-healing mechanisms and adaptive meta-strategies that allow them to handle failure and optimize resource-constrained learning effectively.
actions.lede: Autonomous systems require distinct self-healing and goal-setting architectures to transcend task-specific automation.

This question has come into focus for autonomous systems that algorithmically make decisions under uncertainty. We argue that machine self-confidence—a form of meta-reasoning based on self-assessments of system knowledge about the state of the world, itself, and ability to reason about and execute tasks—leads to many computable and useful competency indicators for such agents. This article presents our body of work, so far, on this concept in the form of the Factorized Machine Self-Confidence (FaMSeC) framework, which holistically considers several major factors driving competency in algorithmic decision-making: outcome assessment, solver quality, model quality, alignment quality, and past experience. In FaMSeC, self-confidence indicators are derived via “problem-solving statistics” embedded in Markov Decision Process solvers and related approaches. These statistics come from evaluating probabilistic exceedance margins in relation to certain outcomes and associated competency standards specified by an evaluator. Once designed, and evaluated, the statistics can be easily incorporated into autonomous agents and serve as indicators of competency. We include detailed descriptions and examples for Markov Decision Process agents and show how outcome assessment and solver quality factors can be found for a range of tasking contexts through novel use of meta-utility functions, behavior simulations, and surrogate prediction models. Traditional models achieve breakthrough performance on language tasks, but do not perform well on basic reasoning benchmarks. However, a new in-context learning approach, Chain-of-thought, has demonstrated strong multi-step reasoning abilities on these benchmarks. The research on LLM reasoning abilities started with the question whether LLMs can solve grade school math word problems, and has expanded to other tasks in the past few years. This article reviews the field of multi-step reasoning with LLMs. We propose a taxonomy that identifies different ways to generate, evaluate, and control multi-step reasoning. We provide an in-depth coverage of core approaches and open problems, and we propose a research agenda for the near future. We find that multi-step reasoning approaches have progressed beyond math word problems, and can now successfully solve challenges in logic, combinatorial games, and robotics, sometimes by first generating code that is then executed by external tools. Many studies in multi-step methods use reinforcement learning for finetuning, external optimization loops, in-context reinforcement learning, and self-reflection.\"}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "2058e547fe3600618a615ea335cdcd06194cf7050f3ec2e3c9d533e7a5515682", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "assumption_challenge", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.1016/s0004-3702(01)00143-6", "doi:10.18653/v1/2026.findings-acl.204", "doi:10.1145/3732794", "doi:10.1145/3774896", "openalex:W2148497685", "openalex:W7166881645", "openalex:W4409887630", "openalex:W4415915064", "arxiv:2407.19631"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.1016/s0004-3702(01)00143-6", "https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0004370201001436/pdf", "https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2026.findings-acl.204", "https://aclanthology.org/2026.findings-acl.204.pdf", "https://doi.org/10.1145/3732794", "https://arxiv.org/pdf/2407.19631", "https://doi.org/10.1145/3774896", "https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/3774896"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}

This article presents our body of work, so far, on this concept in the form of the Factorized Machine Self-Confidence (FaMSeC) framework, which holistically considers several major factors driving competency in algorithmic decision-making: outcome assessment, solver quality, model quality, alignment quality, and past experience. In FaMSeC, self-confidence indicators are derived via “problem-solving statistics” embedded in Markov Decision Process solvers and related approaches. These statistics come from evaluating probabilistic exceedance margins in relation to certain outcomes and associated competency standards specified by an evaluator. Once designed, and evaluated, the statistics can be easily incorporated into autonomous agents and serve as indicators of competency. We include detailed descriptions and examples for Markov Decision Process agents and show how outcome assessment and solver quality factors can be found for a range of tasking contexts through novel use of meta-utility functions, behavior simulations, and surrogate prediction models. Traditional models achieve breakthrough performance on language tasks, but do not perform well on basic reasoning benchmarks. However, a new in-context learning approach, Chain-of-thought, has demonstrated strong multi-step reasoning abilities on these benchmarks. The research on LLM reasoning abilities started with the question whether LLMs can solve grade school math word problems, and has expanded to other tasks in the past few years. This article reviews the field of multi-step reasoning with LLMs. We propose a taxonomy that identifies different ways to generate, evaluate, and control multi-step reasoning. We find that multi-step reasoning approaches have progressed beyond math word problems, and can now successfully solve challenges in logic, combinatorial games, and robotics, sometimes by first generating code that is then executed by external tools.
